segments.text: American Fork City Council — Regular Session — January 23, 2018:

entities.speaker: Darren J. Falslev
entities.remark-context: COPS grant for a school resource officer

segments.text: Chief Falslev described a competitive federal grant that would fund a new junior-high school resource officer for three years. He said the $125,000 award would support community policing and, under the arrangement with the school district, would impose no cost on the city during that period.

entities.speaker: Kevin J. Barnes
entities.remark-context: COPS grant for a school resource officer

segments.text: Council Member Barnes asked whether the city could seek the grant again after three years. After Chief Falslev explained that the grant was offered annually but was highly competitive, Barnes praised the Police Department and called the award a benefit to the community.

entities.speaker: Clark P. Taylor
entities.remark-context: COPS grant for a school resource officer

segments.text: Council Member Taylor credited Chief Falslev’s leadership for the successful school-resource-officer grant and commended his accomplishments as police chief.

entities.speaker: Kevin J. Barnes
entities.remark-context: Police overtime in the Steel Days management agreement

segments.text: Council Member Barnes requested clarification of the $12,000 allocated for police overtime in the Steel Days management agreement.

entities.speaker: Bradley J. Frost
entities.remark-context: State of the City public-safety remarks

segments.text: In his State of the City remarks, Mayor Frost highlighted police call, arrest, and investigation figures; the assignment of a full-time domestic-violence investigator; community education; police use of Narcan; coordinated active-shooter training; and the police chief’s work on state public-safety policy.

entities.label: COPS grant for a school resource officer

segments.text: The council discussed a federal grant for a new school resource officer at American Fork Junior High, the grant’s cost structure, and its longer-term implications.
Relevant discussion from the official meeting minutes:

Police Chief Falslev said this was an important grant for American Fork. It was a highly competitive grant and only 16% of the agencies who applied were successful on obtaining funds. This was also important because they built relationships with the community with implementing community policing. This grant would benefit the Jr. High because that was where they would assign the additional officer. The grant would pay $125,000 over three years in wages and benefits. In negotiating with the school district, there would be no cost to the City for three years.

Council Member Shelton asked if the agreement with the school district continued as long as there was an SRO assigned. The Chief said they intended for this agreement to continue in the future.

Council Member Carroll said she was impressed they were able to get the grant. She asked if they would be hiring a new officer and what would happen the fourth year. Chief Falslev said the fourth year would carry over because they were implementing the money in January instead of the beginning of the new fiscal year. They were either required to re-hire someone who was laid off or hire someone new. In this case they would hire someone new.

Council Member Barnes asked if they could apply for the grant every three years. Chief Falslev said the grant was offered every year; they would apply every year but the process was highly competitive. Council Member Barnes said he was grateful for the police department and remarked that this was a benefit to the community.

Council Member Taylor said he did not think this happened by accident. He commended Chief Falslev for all that he had accomplished during his tenure as Police Chief.
Council Member Barnes requested clarification of police-overtime funding in the Steel Days management agreement.
Relevant discussion from the official meeting minutes:
Council Member Barnes asked if they could clarify the $12,000 overtime for the police department in Section 3.4. He also noted that in Section 4.3 there was a typo that needed to be fixed.

entities.label: State of the City public-safety remarks

segments.text: Mayor Frost discussed police workload, domestic-violence response, overdose response, emergency coordination, and police leadership as part of a broader public-safety address.
Relevant discussion from the official meeting minutes:

Our Police and Fire do much for us. Last year our Police had almost 30,000 service calls, made 233 felony arrests, and averaged 1,252 open investigations. Similarly, our Fire & Rescue handled 2,895 calls for service, which is just under Lehi, who is double our population. These brave men and women have taken an oath to protect and serve. That is there job. But their love of that job and the community has driven them to do much more that what is required. Last year our Police decided to do something about the growing number of domestic violence cases. They assigned one investigator full time to domestic violence cases and began offering public education programs to the community. In fact, I personally worked closely with our Police and Utah County to put together a regional town hall meeting to educate people on the issue and connect those in need to available resources. Our police are often the first call on incidents, but they remain involved, often meeting with many other agencies along the way, to ensure the best outcome of each domestic violence case. In an effort to be proactive our Police and Fire departments started a program where they have equipped and trained our Police officers who are typically first on scene to use Narcan, a drug that can save the lives of those succumbing to a drug overdose. In another example of doing more, our Fire department has begun to train with our Police department so they can provide lifesaving services to injured people DURING an active shooter situation rather than waiting until AFTER it’s safe to go in and triage. Out residents enjoy lower insurance costs thanks in part to the responsiveness to our Fire department. Our Police Chief has taken an active role in legislature that impacts public safety and now sits on a policy making board at the capital. Finally, our Fire department working towards certifying all City employees to be CPR ready. This will dramatically increase our ability to respond in an emergency. The point is, these actions show how our community is in good hands with a Police and Fire department who actively, rather than reactively, serve and protect all of us.
